svg.title: Three places to terminate TLS
svg.desc: Option A, terminate at the load balancer with plain HTTP inside: the client connects over TLS 1.3 to a load balancer that holds the certificate and key, which forwards plain HTTP to TaskFlow API pods on port 3000. Pro: simplest, certificates in one managed place, and the load balancer can inspect HTTP for routing and a web application firewall. Con: traffic between the load balancer and the pods is plaintext, so you must trust the network. Option B, terminate and re-encrypt: the load balancer holds the public certificate and opens a new TLS connection to pods that use internal certificates on port 8443, verified with an internal CA. Pro: encrypted end to end inside your network while the load balancer can still route on HTTP. Con: two certificate systems, and backend verification is often forgotten. Option C, TCP passthrough: a layer 4 load balancer routes by SNI without keys, and the pods hold the public certificate and terminate TLS themselves. Pro: the load balancer never sees keys or plaintext. Con: no HTTP-aware routing, firewall, or header injection at the load balancer, and certificates must reach every pod.

g.text: A. Terminate at the load balancer; plain HTTP inside
B. Terminate and re-encrypt to the backend
C. TCP passthrough: the app terminates TLS
Pro: simplest; certificates in one managed place; the LB can inspect HTTP (routing, WAF).
Con: traffic between the LB and the pods is plaintext; you must trust that network.
Pro: encrypted inside your network too, while the LB can still route on HTTP.
Con: two certificate systems; verifying backend certificates is often forgotten.
Pro: the LB never sees keys or plaintext; TLS runs end to end to the app.
Con: no HTTP-aware routing, WAF, or header injection at the LB; certificates on every pod.
Choose where plaintext is allowed to exist; re-encryption without verification is not authentication.
